newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians vote for mayors, seen as national test.
newsitem.headline: Italians vote for mayors, seen as national test.

text.p: Voters in Italy's financial capital Milan and more than 1,100 towns and cities went to the polls on Sunday for local elections billed as a test of support for the country's centre-left government.

The elections for mayors and municipal councils, involving some 9.4 million voters or about one-fifth of the national electorate, fall one year after Prime Minister Romano Prodi led his Olive Tree coalition to victory in a general election.
The key mayoral battles, in Milan and the big northern cities of Turin and Trieste, are all expected to be decided in second-round run-offs on May 11.

Polling stations opened at seven a.m. (0500 GMT) and were to close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT). Exit polls will forecast the outcome as soon as voting ends but official results were not expected until late on Monday.

The government's popularity has suffered in recent months from resentment at tax hikes it has brought in to rein in the budget deficit and try to squeeze Italy into the first wave of countries to join Europe's planned single currency.

It has sought to divorce Sunday's municipal polls from its own performance, clouded by a battle of wills between centrists in the coalition and the hard left Communist Refoundation party which provides Prodi with his parliamentary majority.
"There is no link between this vote and the government," L'Unita, the newspaper of the big Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), said in an editorial.
But most other editorial writers and the main opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance saw Sunday's vote as a barometer of public sentiment on the Prodi government.
"Victory for the Freedom Alliance could really mean the epilogue for the Prodi government," hard-right leader Gianfranco Fini told a campaign rally on Friday.

In Milan, where a bomb blast at city hall on Friday raised tension ahead of the polls, the contest for mayor is a three-way race between incumbent Marco Formentini of the separatist Northern League and Olive Tree and Freedom Alliance opponents.

Many political analysts expect Formentini to be ousted in the first round in a blow to the prestige of the League, leaving industrialists Gabriele Albertini of the Freedom Alliance and Aldo Fumagalli of the Olive Tree in the race.
The mayoral elections in Turin and Trieste pit incumbent Olive Tree politicians against centre-right rivals.
All three key contests have a host of additional candidates, including from Refoundation.

The Marxist-inspired party's performance will be watched closely for any sign that it has gained support as a result of its resistance to spending cuts in a drive by Prodi to reform the welfare state and Italy's generous pensions system.

Structural reform to the welfare state will be vital to Italy's hopes of reducing the 1998 budget deficit sufficiently to continue to meet the tough deficit criterion needed to stay in Europe's single currency.

Freedom Alliance leader Silvio Berlusconi has used the local election campaign to push his line that such reform will be impossible as long as Prodi needs to rely on Communist Refoundation to pass legislation.

The opposition leader has said he is ready to lend support to Prodi on economic policy if he ditches Refoundation. His overtures have been rejected by the prime minister and the PDS, the biggest force in the government.
